title: India's Supreme Court Just Questioned Its Own Ruling on Umar Khalid. The Implications Go Far Beyond One Case.
excerpt: In a rare act of judicial self-criticism, the Court declared bail the rule under UAPA — and exposed the uncomfortable truth that 98 percent of people charged under the anti-terror law are eventually acquitted.
body:
The Supreme Court of India does not often admit it got something wrong. On May 18, it came as close as the institution allows. A bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan, while granting bail to a Jammu and Kashmir man jailed for nearly six years under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, took the extraordinary step of expressing "serious reservations" about the Court's own January 2026 verdict — the one that denied bail to former JNU student leader Umar Khalid and activist Sharjeel Imam in the Delhi riots conspiracy case.

The implications extend well beyond the fate of two men. The ruling is a direct challenge to how India's most powerful anti-terror legislation has been used — and a rare judicial acknowledgment that the system may be locking people up for years with virtually no chance of conviction.

## The Numbers That Embarrass the State

The most striking element of the judgment is the Court's reliance on hard data. Citing National Crime Records Bureau statistics presented to Parliament by the Union Home Ministry itself, the bench noted that UAPA conviction rates between 2019 and 2023 ranged from a mere 1.5 to 4 percent nationally. In Jammu and Kashmir — where the law is most aggressively deployed — conviction rates never exceeded 0.89 percent, and in 2019 stood at zero.

Justice Bhuyan's arithmetic was blunt: "There is 94 to 98 percent possibility of acquittal in such cases in the country. In Jammu and Kashmir, there is 99 percent possibility of acquittal." The question the Court was posing, without quite saying it directly, was this: what is the moral and constitutional basis for keeping someone in jail for six years when the state's own data shows it almost never proves its case?

## Reversing Course on Khalid

In January 2026, a different two-judge bench — Justices Aravind Kumar and N.V. Anjaria — had handled the bail pleas of multiple accused in the Delhi riots "larger conspiracy" case. That bench granted bail to five co-accused, including Gulfisha Fatima and Meeran Haider, after nearly six years of incarceration. But it denied bail to Khalid and Imam, holding that prosecution material placed them on a "qualitatively different footing" as alleged ideological drivers of the conspiracy.

The May 18 bench did not formally overrule that decision — procedurally, a two-judge bench cannot overrule another two-judge bench. But it went as far as institutional convention permits. Justice Bhuyan wrote that the January verdict in Gulfisha Fatima v. State "would have us believe that Najeeb is only a narrow and exceptional departure" from the statutory restrictions on bail under UAPA. "It is this hollowing out of the import of the observations in Najeeb that we are concerned with."

The reference is to the 2021 three-judge bench decision in Union of India v. KA Najeeb, which established that prolonged incarceration and delayed trials are independent constitutional grounds for granting bail, even under laws with stringent bail restrictions. The May 18 bench reaffirmed that Najeeb remains binding law and warned that smaller benches cannot "dilute, circumvent or disregard" the reasoning of larger benches.

## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention

For Indians abroad, the UAPA debate may seem distant — a domestic Indian legal concern with no direct bearing on NRI life. That reading misses the larger picture. The law's expanding application has drawn attention from international human rights organisations, foreign governments, and global media. Academic conferences, diaspora political discussions, and even investment decisions are increasingly shaped by perceptions of India's civil liberties landscape.

The chilling effect is not theoretical. Indian-origin academics and activists in the US, UK, and Canada have described being cautious about public statements on Indian politics, aware that UAPA charges have been filed against individuals for speeches, social media posts, and participation in protests. The Delhi riots case itself involves allegations rooted in WhatsApp messages and public speeches — the kind of activity that diaspora Indians engage in routinely.

More broadly, the rule-of-law signal matters for India's economic ambitions. Foreign institutional investors, multinational companies considering India operations, and NRIs evaluating return migration all factor legal predictability into their calculations. A Supreme Court that publicly questions the constitutional validity of prolonged pre-trial detention under anti-terror laws sends a different signal than one that rubber-stamps prosecutorial overreach.

## What Happens Next

The immediate beneficiary of the May 18 ruling is Syed Iftikhar Andrabi, the J&K man whose bail plea triggered the judgment. Arrested by the NIA in June 2020 on narco-terror charges, he faced over 320 prosecution witnesses with only a handful examined — making the completion of his trial a distant prospect. The Court ordered his release subject to conditions including passport surrender and fortnightly police reporting.

For Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, the ruling does not automatically translate into freedom. But it significantly strengthens their legal position. Any future bail application can now cite the Court's own "serious reservations" about the judgment that denied them release. The institutional pressure on the January bench — and on any future bench that hears their plea — has shifted.

The larger question is whether the ruling marks a turning point in UAPA jurisprudence or remains an isolated act of judicial conscience. India files more UAPA cases each year than it resolves. The backlog grows. The undertrials wait. And the Court has now put on record that it knows the system is broken — even if it has not yet summoned the will to fix it entirely.
